855.title: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari
855.hook: the Prophet's host in Medina, who, tradition says, was buried at the walls of Constantinople
855.howItsDone: Muslims tell Abu Ayyub's story from Sahih Muslim, where he hosts the Prophet in Medina, and remember him as a model of hospitality.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khabbab, the blacksmith who would not sell his faith for a debt. Your line was the blacksmith endured.

Middle of the night, in a two-story house in Medina. A man wakes and can't get back to sleep, because of where he's lying. Right under his floor, his guest is sleeping, and the guest is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Every step this man and his wife take up here, every shuffle, is over the Prophet's head. So the two of them move into a corner and stay there till morning. Today: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, and what it looks like to take a guest seriously.
screen: `MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.` → `THE GUEST IS DOWNSTAIRS.` → `THEY MOVE INTO A CORNER.`

segments.voice: Sahih Muslim tells it from Abu Ayyub himself. When the Prophet came to Medina, he stayed in Abu Ayyub's house. The Prophet chose the lower floor, and Abu Ayyub's family lived above. After that sleepless night, Abu Ayyub went to him. The lower floor is easier for me, the Prophet explained. I will not go up onto a roof that you are under, Abu Ayyub answered. So the Prophet moved upstairs, and his host moved down. Then the food. Abu Ayyub would send up meals, and when the dish came back, he would ask where the Prophet's fingers had been, and eat from that spot. One day the dish came back untouched. It had garlic in it. Abu Ayyub went up, worried: is it forbidden? No, the Prophet said, but I don't like it. Then, said Abu Ayyub, I dislike what you dislike. That's hosting with attention: noticing the floor, the plate, the smell of garlic. A good host keeps learning the guest. Then the story jumps a long way forward. The Sunan of Abu Dawud places Abu Ayyub with a Muslim army at Constantinople, explaining a verse of the Qur'an to the soldiers there. Tradition says he died on that campaign and asked to be buried as close to the city's walls as they could reach. The man who once wouldn't walk over the Prophet's head ended his life far from that house, still on the road.
screen: `THE LOWER FLOOR IS EASIER FOR ME.` · `NOT ON A ROOF THAT YOU ARE UNDER.` · `I DISLIKE WHAT YOU DISLIKE.` · `FAR AWAY, AT CONSTANTINOPLE.` · then, large: `THE HOST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who will be in your space soon: a visiting relative, a friend for coffee, a child coming home from school. Picture them arriving, and ask what would make it easier for them: a free chair, a drink they like, your phone face down. If you pray, you can ask blessing on the people who come through your door.
Abu Ayyub. The man of Medina whose house sheltered the Prophet, and who, tradition says, was buried near the walls of Constantinople. Today's word.
Your line: the host. The floor, the plate, the garlic: he noticed it all. Until tomorrow.

856.title: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
856.hook: the Ansar chief whose death shook the Throne (Bukhari)
856.howItsDone: Muslims remember Sa'd ibn Mu'adh from reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, above all the Prophet's words that the Throne of the Most Merciful shook at his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Ayyub, who moved downstairs so his guest could sleep above. Your line was the host.

The Throne of the Most Merciful shook. That's the sentence. Jabir ibn Abdullah says he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say it, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it, in a chapter about one man. Not a prophet. Not a king. The chief of a clan in Medina, wounded in battle, who died of the wound. What kind of life gets a sentence like that at its end? Today: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.
screen: `THE THRONE SHOOK.` → `NOT A PROPHET, NOT A KING.` → `WHAT KIND OF LIFE?`

segments.voice: Sa'd was a leader of the Aws, a tribe of Medina, and the early biographies say that when he accepted Islam, his clan followed him. He was a chief, with people looking at him. Bukhari shows what that looked like. Sa'd went to Mecca to perform the umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, staying with an old friend there. Abu Jahl, a leader of the Prophet's opponents, stopped him at the Kaaba and sneered that he was walking around safely after giving shelter to the Prophet's people. Sa'd didn't lower his voice. If you stop me from this, he said, I'll stop you from something worse: your trade road to Syria, which runs past Medina. A chief speaking as a chief, for the people under his protection. At the battle of the Trench, Sa'd was hit by an arrow in the arm; we met the tent where he was cared for, Rufaydah's tent in the mosque. In his last days he was also asked to give a judgment in a hard and painful case, one the histories record and readers still wrestle with; that story needs its own day. The wound did not heal, and he died of it. That's when the Prophet said the Throne shook. Bukhari adds another scene. Someone gave the Prophet a garment of silk, and people kept touching it, amazed at how soft it was. The handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise, the Prophet said, are better than this. A small, everyday thing, finer than the softest thing in the room. Sa'd held one role, chief of his people, and held it the same way in Mecca, in battle, and in a tent with a wound that wouldn't close.
screen: `A CHIEF, WITH PEOPLE WATCHING.` · `FACING ABU JAHL AT THE KAABA.` · `AN ARROW AT THE TRENCH.` · `HANDKERCHIEFS FINER THAN SILK.` · then, large: `THE THRONE SHOOK.`

segments.voice: You hold more than one role: parent, child, friend, worker, neighbor. Choose one and ask where, in it, you are one person in public and another in private, then let one small difference close; not all of them, one. If you pray, you can ask for sincerity, which Muslims call ikhlas, in that one role.
Sa'd. The chief of Medina who stood up to Abu Jahl, was wounded at the Trench, and at whose death, the Prophet said, the Throne shook. Today's word.

857.title: Uways al-Qarani
857.hook: a man from Yemen who never met the Prophet ﷺ, cared for his mother, and whose prayers were sought
857.tomorrow: The women who asked for a day
857.howItsDone: Muslims retell the report in Sahih Muslim of Umar seeking out Uways and asking for his prayer, and often hold him up as an example of devotion to a parent and of a hidden, humble life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sa'd, the chief of the Ansar. Your line was the throne shook.

Every time a fresh group of fighters arrives in Medina from Yemen, Umar ibn al-Khattab goes out to meet them with the same question. Is Uways ibn Amir among you? Again and again, no. Umar leads the whole community by now, and still he keeps asking after one man he has never seen. Then one day a voice in the crowd says yes. Umar walks up to him and asks his own favor: pray for me. Today: Uways al-Qarani.
screen: `IS UWAYS AMONG YOU?` → `AGAIN AND AGAIN, NO.` → `THEN ONE DAY, YES.`

segments.voice: The story is in Sahih Muslim, and Umar tells us why he kept asking. He had heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, describe a man who would come with the reinforcements from Yemen: Uways ibn Amir, of the tribe of Murad, then of the clan of Qaran. He had suffered a skin disease and been cured of it, except for one small patch. And he had a mother, and he was devoted to her. Then something remarkable: if this man swore by God, God would make his oath come true. If you meet him, ask him to seek forgiveness for you. So Umar checks every detail, and Uways confirms them all: Murad, Qaran, the healed skin, the mother. Then Umar, the companion of the Prophet, asks a man who never met the Prophet to pray for him. And Uways does. Why did he never meet him? The hadith only says he was dutiful to his mother. Tradition says that is exactly what kept him in Yemen: she needed him, and he stayed. That link is the tradition's, not the hadith's words. Then the end of the conversation. Umar asks where he is going. Kufa, says Uways. Umar offers to write to the governor there for him, and Uways declines. He would rather be among the ordinary people, the ones nobody notices. He had a recommendation from the leader of the believers in his hand, and he let it go. The man whose prayer was sought was the man who did not seek to be seen. And in the Prophet's description, the one deed named is not a battle or a speech. It is his care for his mother.
screen: `DESCRIBED BY THE PROPHET.` · `DEVOTED TO HIS MOTHER.` · `UMAR ASKS HIM TO PRAY.` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY UNNOTICED.` · then, large: `HE STAYED WITH HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your mother or father, or whoever raised you, and one ordinary thing they need right now: a call, a ride, a meal, ten minutes of listening without your phone. If your parent has died, hold them in mind instead and, if you pray, ask mercy for them. If the relationship is hard, choose something small and safe, or simply wish them well.

858.title: The women who asked for a day
858.hook: women asked the Prophet ﷺ for a day to teach them, and he gave it
858.howItsDone: Muslims cite this report from Sahih al-Bukhari when talking about women's study of the religion, and mosques and communities hold classes and circles for women.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uways, the man of Yemen whose prayer Umar sought. Your line was he stayed with his mother.

A complaint, made out loud, to the Prophet himself. The men, a group of women tell him, have taken all of your time. Every gathering, every lesson, the men are there first, crowding in. So the women make a request: set aside a day for us, just for us, when we can come and learn from you. It's a few lines in Sahih al-Bukhari, the kind of request that could be brushed off with a vague promise. Today: the women who asked for a day.
screen: `THE MEN HAVE TAKEN YOUR TIME.` → `SET ASIDE A DAY FOR US.` → `WHAT WILL HE SAY?`

segments.voice: Bukhari places this report in his book on knowledge, narrated by the companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The women come to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and name the problem plainly. They don't ask for a favor. They ask for a day. And the hadith says he promised them one, and kept it: he met them on that day, and he advised them and taught them. So teaching was not something that happened to women by accident, overheard from the back of a room. When they asked, a time was made for them on purpose, and the Prophet showed up. Then a glimpse of what was said. He told them that a woman who loses three of her children will find them a shield for her from the Fire. And one woman, in the middle of the lesson, asks: and two? He says: and two. These women brought their real lives into the room, including the grief of losing a child, and the teaching met them there. And a woman felt free to interrupt and ask about her own case. That is a day for learning: a set time, a teacher who arrives, and room for the question you actually have. In the same book on knowledge, Aisha is remembered praising the women of the Ansar, because shyness did not stop them from learning their religion. The request for a day sits in that company.

859.title: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari
859.hook: a companion whose recitation the Prophet ﷺ likened to the pipes of the family of Dawud
859.howItsDone: Muslims value beautiful, careful recitation of the Qur'an (tajwid), and Abu Musa's reported gift comes up when people speak of reciting with a lovely voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the women of the Ansar who asked for a day. Your line was a day for learning.

Night in Medina. A man is reciting the Qur'an, for no one in particular. He doesn't know that out in the dark, someone has stopped to listen. The next day the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells him: if only you had seen me last night, listening to your recitation. Then a compliment: you have been given one of the pipes of the family of Dawud. Today: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a man from Yemen with a voice worth stopping for.
screen: `RECITING AT NIGHT, ALONE.` → `SOMEONE STOPS TO LISTEN.` → `A PIPE OF DAWUD'S FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The word in the hadith is mizmar, a reed pipe, a wind instrument. Dawud, the prophet David, is remembered in the Qur'an as one with whom the mountains and the birds joined in praise. So the Prophet was saying: your voice carries something of that. Muslim and Bukhari both record it. But here's the turn. Abu Musa also narrates a very different lesson about voices. On a journey, he reports, the companions were climbing and calling out God is greatest at the top of their lungs. And the Prophet told them to go easy on themselves. You are not calling on someone deaf or absent, he said. You are calling on One who hears, and who is near. Put the two reports side by side. The sweet voice was heard at night, unplanned, not on a stage. The loud voices were gently quieted. Beauty in recitation, in these reports, is not about volume. It's about a sense that the One addressed is close. A third picture of Abu Musa's people fits. Bukhari records the Prophet praising the Ash'aris, Abu Musa's tribe, because when their food ran low they gathered everything they had on one cloth and shared it out equally. They are from me, he said, and I am from them. A people known for sharing, and one of them known for a voice. Neither the food nor the voice was kept to themselves.

segments.voice: If you know a short surah, or al-Fatiha, say it now almost under your breath, slowly, giving each letter its place and not rushing the long vowels. If you don't recite, do the same with any words that matter to you, or simply listen to your breathing as if it were a sound worth tending. Not loud. Close, as if speaking to someone who is near.

860.title: Hudhayfah, keeper of secrets
860.hook: the keeper of secrets, who asked about harm so he could avoid it
860.howItsDone: Muslims quote Hudhayfah's words about asking of evil in order to avoid it, and scholars cite his long report in Bukhari when discussing how to hold fast during times of trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Musa, whose recitation the Prophet heard in the night. Your line was a voice like Dawud's.

What brings reward? What is best? Those were the questions people brought to the Prophet. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, a companion, later tells his listeners how his own questions ran the other way. People used to ask the Messenger of God about the good, he says. I used to ask him about the evil, because I was afraid it would catch me. Plenty of us collect advice about what to do. Hudhayfah collected warnings. Today: Hudhayfah.
screen: `THEY ASKED ABOUT THE GOOD.` → `HE ASKED ABOUT THE EVIL.` → `AFRAID IT WOULD CATCH HIM.`

segments.voice: That sentence opens a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari. Hudhayfah asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: we were in ignorance and harm, and God brought us this good. Will there be harm after this good? Yes, the Prophet says. And after that harm, good again? Yes, but with some smoke in it, some haze. Hudhayfah keeps pressing for the next turn and the next, until he asks the practical one: if that time reaches me, what do you command me to do? The point of all the asking was not gloom. It was a plan: find out where the road gets dangerous so you can walk around it. His fellow companions noticed something else. In Bukhari, Abu al-Darda refers to Hudhayfah as the one among them who holds the secret that no one else knows. Tradition says the Prophet had told him things he told no one else, including who among the people of Medina were hypocrites, and that Hudhayfah kept it. Some reports say even Umar would ask him, worried, whether his own name was on that list, and that Hudhayfah would only say no to him, and name no one else. Those details come from later reports, not from Bukhari. So the man who asked about harm was also trusted with hard knowledge, and he didn't spend it on gossip. Knowing where the danger was did not make him suspicious of everyone. It made him careful with himself, and quiet about others.

segments.voice: Ask yourself Hudhayfah's question, pointed inward: where does harm usually catch me? A certain hour of the night, a certain app, a conversation that always turns sour, anger when I'm hungry. Don't scold yourself; just name it, the way you'd mark a pothole on your street, and if you pray, ask for protection from it.
Hudhayfah. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, the companion who asked the Prophet about harm so he could avoid it, remembered as the keeper of secrets. Today's word.

861.title: Salim, Mu'adh and the others
861.hook: four the Prophet ﷺ named as teachers of the Qur'an: Ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh and Ubayy
861.howItsDone: Muslims learn to recite the Qur'an from a teacher face to face, and chains of recitation are traced back through companions such as Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hudhayfah, who asked about harm so he could avoid it. Your line was ask about the harm.

A short list. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once named the people to go to if you wanted to learn the Qur'an: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Salim the freed man of Abu Hudhayfah, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Three of those names have had a day of their own on this path already. One hasn't. And he's the one who, on paper, didn't belong: a man who had once been owned, whose name in the hadith is tied to someone else's. Today: Salim.
screen: `LEARN THE QUR'AN FROM FOUR.` → `THREE YOU'VE MET.` → `ONE YOU HAVEN'T.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abdullah ibn Amr: learn the Qur'an from four. Alongside the other three stands Salim, whose title is mawla, a word that here means a freed man still linked to the household that freed him. Tradition says Abu Hudhayfah took him in as a son. In the hadith, his name doesn't stand alone. And the Prophet sent people to him anyway. Bukhari also records what happened at Quba, before the Prophet himself reached Medina. When the first emigrants arrived, Salim led them in prayer, and the report gives the reason: he knew the most Qur'an of them. Not the best family. Not the most wealth. The most Qur'an. So the men who had left Mecca stood behind a freed man, because of what he carried in his memory. The biographies, not Bukhari, add that Salim was later killed at the battle of Yamamah, carrying the emigrants' banner. What the hadith gives for certain is the list, and the list is a kind of permission. It tells anyone who wants to learn: go to the ones who know, whoever they are. And it tells anyone who teaches, whatever their past: what you carry matters more than the name you were given. That closes a week of companions: Abu Ayyub the host, Sa'd and the throne, Uways and his mother, the Ansar women, Abu Musa's voice, Hudhayfah's questions, and now Salim at the front of the line in Quba.

segments.voice: Bring to mind whoever taught you to read the Qur'an, or taught you al-Fatiha, the prayer, or the first Arabic letters: a parent, a teacher at the mosque, a friend, an app voice, even. If you never had one, think of whoever first taught you something you still use every day. Thank them in your mind, and if you pray, ask good for them.
